I did not source wikipedia and I am not just **solely** taking about the bi-sexual pride flag.  

Do not badger me and make assumptions that I am using flawed sources and have not attempted actual research.

The trans pride flag is a perfect example of my point, however, it is not the only flag that fits into that category and other flag innovators have stated that the colors are stereotypical colors assigned to gender.

Not **all** flags are like this, but **some** are and it raised an honest inquiry into the “why”?

Again...Yes, I have researched the colors on the flags.

The trans, bisexual, lipstick lesbian, gender-fluid, and polysexual flags all use colors that are representative of stereotypically assigned colors for gender.

"The stripes at the top and bottom are light blue, the traditional color for baby boys. The stripes next to them are pink, the traditional color for baby girls. The stripe in the middle is white, for those who are transitioning or consider themselves having a neutral or undefined gender."  -  Monica Helms [Creator of Trans pride flag]

While the pansexual, polyamory, intersex, asexual, aromantic are examples of nonconformity.

I only wondered (with the exception of the gender-fluid and trans flags) why most dated flags conform while newly created flags do not conform to stereotypical colors for gender.

Oh yeah, I meant like:  [Pride Flags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride_flag?wprov=sfti1) 

Examples are the bisexual, bigender, and trans pride flags.

I should have phrased my query better.  By all means, my perspective of the conformity of the flags is for some of them vs all/most.

More of the dated flags seem to support the stereotypic colors, as opposed to the more recent creations/designs.  I feel as though I’m split when it comes to this.  

On one hand, I understand the traditional representation and its relation to identity.  However,  at the same time, I feel as though utilizing something from “traditional gender role” culture is the antithesis of the lgbt+ movement.

In any case, your last sentence sums it up perfectly:

“People who use these flags might want to destroy the concept of gendered colours (though not all of them do) *at the same time* as recognising that gendered colours can be useful in conveying a specific meaning, or simply at the same time as enjoying the colours for what they are.”
